posts.title: Why Can't Countries Just Print More Money?
posts.text:
Why can't a government just print money to make everyone rich? We break it down with a tiny island economy, Zimbabwe's 100 trillion dollar note, and the US money supply growing about 40% in two years, and explain why the US avoided hyperinflation.

Zimbabwe's prices doubled roughly every 25 hours at the peak (79.6 billion percent a month in November 2008). The US printed trillions too, and inflation hit 9.1%, the highest in 40 years, but not hyperinflation. Here are the four reasons, the "brake" central banks use, and why most of them aim for 2% inflation.

Chapters
0:00 The $100 trillion note
0:30 An island with ten loaves
1:17 Money isn't wealth
1:30 What happened in Zimbabwe
2:11 The US printed too
2:44 Four reasons the US was different
3:37 The brake and the 2% target
4:04 Who controls the printing press
4:34 You can't print bread

Sources
Hanke and Kwok, "On the Measurement of Zimbabwe's Hyperinflation", Cato Journal, 2009: cato.org/sites/cato.org/files/serials/files/cato-journal/2009/5/cj29n2-8.pdf
BBC News, "Zimbabwe rolls out Z$100tr note", 16 January 2009
BBC News, "Zimbabwe dollar 'not back soon'", 12 April 2009
Federal Reserve H.6 Money Stock Measures (M2), via FRED: fred.stlouisfed.org/series/M2SL
US Bureau of Labor Statistics, "Consumer prices up 9.1 percent over the year ended June 2022": bls.gov/opub/ted/2022/consumer-prices-up-9-1-percent-over-the-year-ended-june-2022-largest-increase-in-40-years.htm
IMF, Currency Composition of Official Foreign Exchange Reserves (COFER), 2026 Q1: data.imf.org
Federal Reserve, Statement on Longer-Run Goals and Monetary Policy Strategy

The island economy is a simplified example. The 40% is the growth of the money supply (M2), not of prices.
Music: "Pizzicato Polka" (Strauss), licensed via Envato Elements.

Previous video: The Money in Your Bank Account Doesn't Exist.
Next: a new series, "How They Take Your Money", starting with sportsbooks.

This video is for education only and is not financial advice.

posts.title: This $100 Trillion Note Was Worth $30 #shorts
posts.text:
Zimbabwe issued a 100 trillion dollar note in January 2009. On its first day it was worth about 30 US dollars. At the peak, prices rose 79.6 billion percent a month and doubled every 24.7 hours. Who decides how much money gets printed, and why is it kept away from politicians?
Sources: BBC News (2009); Hanke and Kwok, Cato Journal (2009).

Full explanation: the related video linked above.
Education only, not financial advice.

posts.title: Why Not Just Print More Money? #shorts
posts.text:
Imagine an island with 10 loaves of bread and 10 dollars: each loaf costs $1. The government prints 10 more dollars. Everyone has twice the money, but there are still only 10 loaves, so the price moves toward $2. Nobody got richer. Money isn't wealth: bread is. You can print money. You can't print bread.
(The island is a simplified example.)

Full explanation: the related video linked above.
Education only, not financial advice.

#money #inflation #economics

Why can't a country just print more money? 🍞

Picture an island: 10 loaves, 10 dollars, $1 a loaf. Print 10 more dollars and everyone has twice the money, but there are still only 10 loaves. The price moves toward $2. Nobody got richer.

You can print money. You can't print bread.

(Simplified example.) Full video on YouTube (link in bio). Education, not financial advice.

posts.title: The US Printed Trillions. Why No Hyperinflation? #shorts
posts.text:
US money (M2) went from $15.5 trillion in February 2020 to $21.8 trillion in March 2022: up 40.6%. Inflation came (9.1% in June 2022, the highest in 40 years), but not hyperinflation. Four reasons: timing, the whole world wants dollars (57% of reserves), the US borrows in its own currency, and trust in an independent central bank.
Sources: Federal Reserve H.6 via FRED; US Bureau of Labor Statistics; IMF COFER (2026 Q1).

Full explanation: the related video linked above.
Education only, not financial advice.

#money #inflation #economics

posts.text:
The US printed trillions of dollars too. So why didn't it become Zimbabwe? 🇺🇸

US money supply: $15.5T (Feb 2020) to $21.8T (Mar 2022), up 40.6%. Inflation hit 9.1% in June 2022, the highest in 40 years, but nowhere near hyperinflation. Four reasons: timing, global demand for dollars, debt in its own currency, and trust.

Sources: Federal Reserve H.6 via FRED; BLS; IMF COFER (2026 Q1).
Full video on YouTube (link in bio). Education, not financial advice.

posts.title: Zimbabwe vs the US: How Fast Is Too Fast? #shorts
posts.text:
Zimbabwe printed money to pay its bills while the economy shrank: 79.6 billion percent inflation a month. The US printed too, and got 9.1%. The difference is speed. Central banks aim for about 2% inflation a year, and use higher interest rates as the brake when money grows faster than the economy.
Sources: Hanke and Kwok (2009); Federal Reserve H.6 via FRED; US Bureau of Labor Statistics; Federal Reserve.

Full explanation: the related video linked above.
Education only, not financial advice.
